subject: Climate & Environment
title: The Global Waste Trade
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Global Waste Trade.

hook.text: For decades, wealthy nations shipped their recycling to China. In 2018, China said no more.

buildup.text: China's National Sword policy banned 24 types of waste imports, shocking the global system.

discovery.text: Waste quickly redirected to Southeast Asia. Vietnam, Malaysia, and Thailand were overwhelmed.

twist.text: Much of the exported recycling was actually too contaminated to recycle. It was dumped or burned.

climax.text: Countries are now forced to handle their own waste — exposing how little they actually recycle.

punchline.text: We weren't recycling. We were just shipping the problem somewhere else.

quiz.question: What was China's National Sword policy?
options: A ban on importing most foreign waste

details.summary: Wealthy countries have long exported millions of tonnes of plastic, paper, and electronic waste to developing nations for processing or disposal. China's 2018 ban on waste imports disrupted this trade, revealing that many exporting countries had not built adequate domestic recycling capacity.
details.whyItMatters: The waste trade offloads environmental burdens onto poorer countries. Understanding it exposes inequities in global waste management and the need for domestic recycling infrastructure.
takeaways: Wealthy nations ship millions of tonnes of waste abroad
China's 2018 import ban disrupted the global waste trade
Many exporting countries lack domestic recycling capacity

faq.question: Why did China ban waste imports?
faq.answer: China received about half the world's recyclable waste for decades, but contamination rates were rising. The National Sword policy banned 24 categories of waste imports to protect domestic health and environment, forcing exporting countries to handle their own waste.

faq.question: Where does waste go now that China has closed its doors?
faq.answer: Exports shifted to Southeast Asian countries like Malaysia, Vietnam, and Indonesia, which quickly became overwhelmed and imposed their own restrictions. Some waste is now landfilled or incinerated domestically. The disruption has spurred investment in local recycling capacity.
